nodes.name: Socket Programming
nodes.explanation: API facilitating bi-directional network communication channels between processes over IP networks.
nodes.real_world_use: Powers backend web servers, chat servers, and microservice RPC communication.

nodes.name: TCP Flow Control
nodes.explanation: Sliding window protocol preventing a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver's buffer.
nodes.real_world_use: Guarantees reliable video streaming and file transfers over variable speed connections.

nodes.name: Packet Encapsulation
nodes.explanation: Wrapping higher-layer data payloads with protocol headers at each OSI layer.
nodes.real_world_use: Enables heterogeneous internet routers to forward payloads without inspecting contents.

nodes.name: DNS Resolution
nodes.explanation: Hierarchical distributed database translating human domain names to numerical IP addresses.
nodes.real_world_use: Every web browser navigation begins with a recursive DNS lookup query.

nodes.name: BGP Routing
nodes.explanation: Path-vector exterior gateway protocol coordinating packet routes across autonomous systems.
nodes.real_world_use: Forms the global backbone routing table linking ISPs worldwide.

nodes.name: System Calls
nodes.explanation: Programmatic interface allowing user programs to request privileged kernel services.
nodes.real_world_use: Every file read, process fork, and network transmit requires invoking a system call.

nodes.name: Virtual Memory & Paging
nodes.explanation: Memory management mapping virtual addresses to physical frames with secondary swap.
nodes.real_world_use: Allows machines to execute programs larger than available physical RAM.

nodes.name: Mutex & Semaphore
nodes.explanation: Synchronization primitives preventing concurrent race conditions in shared critical sections.
nodes.real_world_use: Coordinates thread safety in multi-threaded browser engines and databases.

nodes.name: Process Scheduling
nodes.explanation: Kernel algorithm allocating CPU time slices among runnable execution threads.
nodes.real_world_use: Linux CFS scheduler balances interactive GUI latency with background compute throughput.

nodes.name: File System Inodes
nodes.explanation: Data structure storing metadata, permissions, and disk block pointers for filesystem objects.
nodes.real_world_use: Underlies POSIX filesystems like ext4 in Android and Linux servers.

nodes.name: Buffer Pool Management
nodes.explanation: In-memory cache manager maintaining fixed-size disk frame pages with LRU eviction.
nodes.real_world_use: Ensures database engines avoid disk I/O on frequently accessed table pages.

nodes.name: Two-Phase Locking (2PL)
nodes.explanation: Concurrency protocol guaranteeing serializability via expanding and shrinking lock phases.
nodes.real_world_use: Enforces strict ACID transaction isolation in financial banking databases.

nodes.name: B+ Tree Indexing
nodes.explanation: Balanced N-ary search tree optimized for disk block reads and high-speed range queries.
nodes.real_world_use: Default primary and secondary index storage engine in MySQL and PostgreSQL.

nodes.name: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)
nodes.explanation: Durability mechanism logging data modifications to append-only disk before applying to tables.
nodes.real_world_use: Guarantees crash recovery without losing committed financial transactions.

nodes.name: Query Optimization
nodes.explanation: Cost-based optimizer selecting optimal relational join algorithms and index paths.
nodes.real_world_use: Transforms declarative SQL queries into low-latency execution plans.

nodes.name: CPU Cache Hierarchy
nodes.explanation: Multi-tier SRAM memory (L1/L2/L3) caching instructions and data close to processor cores.
nodes.real_world_use: Reduces CPU memory latency from 100ns (DRAM) to sub-nanosecond L1 speeds.

nodes.name: Direct Memory Access (DMA)
nodes.explanation: Hardware subsystem enabling I/O devices to transfer data directly to RAM without CPU overhead.
nodes.real_world_use: High-throughput NVMe drives and 100Gbps network cards stream directly to host memory.

nodes.name: Instruction Pipelining
nodes.explanation: Instruction-level parallelism breaking instruction execution into staggered overlapping stages.
nodes.real_world_use: Dramatically boosts CPU throughput in modern x86 and ARM processors.

nodes.name: Interrupt Handling
nodes.explanation: Hardware signal diverting CPU execution to dedicated Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs).
nodes.real_world_use: Enables asynchronous hardware notifications from keyboard, mouse, and network devices.

nodes.name: Memory Management Unit (MMU)
nodes.explanation: Hardware component translating virtual addresses to physical addresses using page tables and TLB.
nodes.real_world_use: Hardware anchor enforcing memory protection and process isolation across operating systems.

links.reason: Network socket APIs (socket, bind, listen, accept) invoke kernel system calls to transfer network packets through device drivers.
links.industry_example: Nginx web servers make non-blocking epoll system calls to accept high volumes of incoming TCP network connections.

evidence.snippet: Socket programming relies on OS abstraction layers to read and write bytes over transport layer TCP connections.
System calls bridge user space applications to kernel-space network protocol stacks and device drivers.

links.snippet_a: Socket programming relies on OS abstraction layers to read and write bytes over transport layer TCP connections.
links.snippet_b: System calls bridge user space applications to kernel-space network protocol stacks and device drivers.

links.reason: The hardware MMU is the physical prerequisite providing page translation and page fault exceptions to the OS pager.
links.industry_example: ARM Cortex and x86 MMU circuits raise page fault exceptions that transfer execution directly to Linux page swap handlers.

evidence.snippet: The MMU hardware contains the page table walker and TLB translating virtual CPU addresses.
Operating systems configure hardware page directory registers so the MMU can perform address translation.

links.snippet_a: The MMU hardware contains the page table walker and TLB translating virtual CPU addresses.
links.snippet_b: Operating systems configure hardware page directory registers so the MMU can perform address translation.

links.reason: Both manage fixed-size memory frames (pages vs buffer frames) and apply eviction policies like LRU when main memory is exhausted.
links.industry_example: PostgreSQL buffer manager implements clock-sweep eviction to cache 8KB table disk blocks in RAM similarly to OS page replacement.

evidence.snippet: Paging divides virtual memory into fixed 4KB chunks, swapping pages between RAM and swap disk when physical capacity is reached.
The database buffer manager maintains an in-memory frame cache of disk pages to minimize expensive secondary storage I/O.

links.snippet_a: Paging divides virtual memory into fixed 4KB chunks, swapping pages between RAM and swap disk when physical capacity is reached.
links.snippet_b: The database buffer manager maintains an in-memory frame cache of disk pages to minimize expensive secondary storage I/O.

links.reason: Hardware atomic primitives (test-and-set, compare-and-swap) and cache coherency protocols (MESI) provide the hardware synchronization foundation for OS mutexes.
links.industry_example: Linux kernel futexes use atomic compare-and-swap CPU instructions to acquire locks in user space without kernel transition if uncontended.

evidence.snippet: Hardware atomic read-modify-write memory operations require cache line locking or bus lock arbitration.
Operating system mutexes and spinlocks use atomic hardware CPU instructions to prevent race conditions across parallel threads.

links.snippet_a: Hardware atomic read-modify-write memory operations require cache line locking or bus lock arbitration.
links.snippet_b: Operating system mutexes and spinlocks use atomic hardware CPU instructions to prevent race conditions across parallel threads.

links.reason: Both apply concurrency control barriers to guarantee serialized execution and prevent dirty reads / data corruption during concurrent execution.
links.industry_example: Financial database transaction engines acquire exclusive record locks following rigorous 2PL protocols to guarantee serializability.

evidence.snippet: Two-Phase Locking ensures conflict serializability by requiring transactions to acquire all locks in a growing phase before releasing any.
Mutual exclusion semaphores ensure that only one concurrent thread enters a critical code section at any given time.

links.snippet_a: Two-Phase Locking ensures conflict serializability by requiring transactions to acquire all locks in a growing phase before releasing any.
links.snippet_b: Mutual exclusion semaphores ensure that only one concurrent thread enters a critical code section at any given time.

links.reason: Network Interface Cards (NICs) transfer incoming packet frames directly into host RAM via DMA without CPU cycle overhead.
links.industry_example: High-speed 10GbE network cards utilize ring buffers and DMA transfers to ingest line-rate packets into kernel memory.

evidence.snippet: DMA controllers bypass the central processor to transfer blocks of peripheral data directly into physical system memory.
Network interface adapters use DMA to offload frame transfer from the CPU during packet transmission.

links.snippet_a: DMA controllers bypass the central processor to transfer blocks of peripheral data directly into physical system memory.
links.snippet_b: Network interface adapters use DMA to offload frame transfer from the CPU during packet transmission.

links.reason: Both systems use graph path cost models (AS-path length vs join tree disk I/O costs) to pick optimal transmission routes.
links.industry_example: Distributed database partition query engines evaluate network hop latency similarly to routing protocols.

evidence.snippet: BGP algorithms evaluate path metrics to find the most cost-effective autonomous system transit.
Relational query optimizers calculate CPU and I/O cost formulas to evaluate join order permutations.

links.snippet_a: BGP algorithms evaluate path metrics to find the most cost-effective autonomous system transit.
links.snippet_b: Relational query optimizers calculate CPU and I/O cost formulas to evaluate join order permutations.

links.reason: Both structures use hierarchical tree path resolution (domain dots vs directory slashes) to resolve human-readable labels to binary addresses.
links.industry_example: Apache and Nginx virtual host mapping converts DNS hostname headers directly to root filesystem directory paths.

evidence.snippet: DNS resolves hostnames hierarchically from root down to top-level domains.
Linux filesystem directories resolve paths starting from root inode down to leaf files.

links.snippet_a: DNS resolves hostnames hierarchically from root down to top-level domains.
links.snippet_b: Linux filesystem directories resolve paths starting from root inode down to leaf files.

evidence.snippet: BGP routers encapsulate path attributes in TCP port 179 packets.

links.reason: Open/read system calls look up disk blocks via inodes.

evidence.snippet: The sys_open call resolves paths by traversing directory inodes.

links.snippet_a: The sys_open call resolves paths by traversing directory inodes.

links.reason: Blocked mutexes yield CPU time slices to runnable threads.

evidence.snippet: Threads waiting on unavailable mutexes enter sleep queues.

links.snippet_a: Threads waiting on unavailable mutexes enter sleep queues.

links.reason: Dirty buffer pool pages cannot be flushed until WAL records are written.

evidence.snippet: WAL protocol guarantees changes are durable before page flush.

links.snippet_a: WAL protocol guarantees changes are durable before page flush.

links.reason: Optimizer evaluates index scan costs vs sequential table scans.

evidence.snippet: Cost models calculate leaf-page depth to determine index feasibility.

evidence.snippet: Translation Lookaside Buffers cache page table entries in hardware.
